Stress may only occur iii certain locations: some stems have penultimate stress, some have final stress, and a handful of borrowings have antepenultimate stress. The addition of a suffix to a stem normally draws the stress one syllable to the right." ... p. 335: "the distinction between closed and open syllables is referred to in the Ilokano stress system: all native words with closed penults have final stress (see Vanoverbergh (1955: 28-29)." fn. 3: "In the dialect we describe, this final stress may optionally retract to the penult, so that native words with closed penults have vacillating stress." || Swift 1909: 17-18: "Accents are of two kinds, radical and accidental. audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are present verbatim (modulo layout whitespace and flagged scanned artifacts) in the copies we hold at the stated locators: Hayes & Abad 1989 pp. 333-335 with fn. 3, and Swift 1909 pp. 17-18. (2) The classification rests on a 1989 Lingua phonology article by Hayes with a native-speaker co-author, corroborated by a 1909 pedagogical grammar; the article treats stress as background and defers to Vanoverbergh 1955, but its statements are explicit and authoritative. (3) I downloaded the open Rosetta excerpt of Rubino's 2005 'Iloko' chapter (phonology section): sec. 2.2 says 'Stress is phonemic.. Stress falls on the last syllable if the penultimate syllable is closed', with loan/velar-nasal exceptions and automatic lengthening of stressed open vowels. sources.quote: "Stress is phonemic, e.g. siká 'you, familiar' vs. síka 'dysentery'. There, are, however, certain environments that attract stress. Stress falls on the last syllable if the penultimate syllable is closed, i.e., the last vowel is preceded by two consonants (including a sequence of glottal stop + consonant): paltóg 'gun', takkí 'excrement' ... Exceptions to this rule include words of foreign origin or words with a velar nasal coda preceding a final syllable: súngka, bibíngka, karámba (Spanish loan), kuárto (Spanish loan).
